facts.text: The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Ankara.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Ankara.

facts.text: The National Intelligence Service began to record telephone conversations of S.K., a Greek attaché in Izmir, and noticed suspicious calls with the applicant, initiating an investigation.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  On an unspecified date, the National Intelligence Service (Milli İstihbarat Teşkilatı, hereinafter MIT) began to record the telephone conversations of S.K., a Greek attaché working at the Consulate of Greece in Izmir and allegedly a member of the Greek Intelligence Service (EIP). The authorities noticed suspicious telephone conversations between S.K. and the applicant and initiated an investigation concerning the applicant.

facts.text: On 18 February 1998 a military prosecutor and MIT officers searched the applicant’s shop in Istanbul and found photographs of military bases, two maps (one marked 'top secret'), and telephone and credit cards.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  On 18 February 1998 a military prosecutor and MIT officers searched the applicant’s shop in Istanbul. According to the preliminary investigation report, several photographs of military bases, two maps (one of which was marked as “top secret”) and telephone and credit cards were found in the shop.

facts.text: V.A.Ö. was present during the search and told MIT officers that the photos belonged to the applicant, not to him.

anchor.surface_text: V.A.Ö. was present when MIT officers carried out a search in the applicant’s shop and told them that the photos of the military bases did not belong to him but to the applicant.

facts.text: The applicant was taken into custody on suspicion of transmitting official and confidential information to Greek intelligence service members and was examined by doctor N.A., who noted he was in good health.

anchor.surface_text: The latter was then taken into custody on suspicion of transmitting official and confidential information to Greek intelligence service members. He was brought before a doctor, N.A., who noted that he was in good health.

facts.text: During custody, the applicant was allegedly subjected to ill-treatment by MIT officers.

anchor.surface_text: During his custody period, the applicant was allegedly subjected to ill‑treatment by the MIT officers.

facts.text: On 20 February 1998 the applicant was brought before the 3rd Army Corps Command Military Court and denied giving confidential information, stating maps and photos did not belong to him.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  On 20 February 1998 the applicant was brought before the 3rd Army Corps Command Military Court. Before this court, he maintained that he had met someone who worked at the Consulate of Greece in Istanbul and that he had sold this person books and silver accessories. He received money from this person for what he had sold. The applicant further contended that this person asked him to provide military information about Turkey. The applicant denied the allegation that he had given confidential information to this person. He stated that the maps and the photographs found in his shop did not belong to him.

facts.text: On 20 February 1998 the court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand and he was examined again by doctor N.A., who found no signs of ill-treatment.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  On the same day, the court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. He was then examined by N.A. who once again noted that there was no trace of ill-treatment on the applicant’s body.

facts.text: The applicant was remanded in Davutpaşa Military Prison and filed an objection to the detention order.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant was then remanded in the Davutpaşa Military Prison. He filed an objection to the detention order.

facts.text: On 23 February 1998 the applicant underwent a third medical examination in prison, which noted ecchymoses on both arms possibly three to four days old.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On 23 February 1998, following his objection to the findings contained in the previous medical reports, the applicant underwent a third medical examination in prison. According to the prison doctor’s report, the applicant had ecchymoses on both arms, which were possibly three to four days old.

facts.text: On 5 March 1998 the applicant filed a further objection to the detention order, which was dismissed by the Navy Command Military Court.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  On 5 March 1998 the applicant filed a further objection to the detention order. On the same day the Navy Command Military Court dismissed his objection.

facts.text: On 19 March 1998 the General Staff Military Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment charging the applicant with disloyalty to national defence by espionage under military and criminal codes.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On 19 March 1998 the General Staff Military Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the General Staff Military Court, charging the applicant under Article 56 § 1 (D) of the Military Criminal Code and Articles 133 § 1, 31, 33 and 36 of the Criminal Code, with disloyalty to national defence by way of espionage.

facts.text: The applicant claimed he was coerced by MIT officers into signing a statement, had sold the shop to V.A.Ö., and that photos and maps did not belong to him.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  The applicant maintained before the General Staff Military Court that he had been coerced by MIT officers into signing a statement while in custody. He claimed that he had sold the shop to V.A.Ö. and that the photographs and maps did not belong to him.

facts.text: The applicant requested V.A.Ö. be heard by the court; he also contended the search was illegal and he was not informed of charges during the search.

anchor.surface_text: He requested that V.A.Ö. be heard by the court. He further contended that the search in the shop was illegal and that he had not been informed of the charges against him by the officials who had conducted the search.

facts.text: The applicant stated he sold books and silver accessories to Greek officials L.K. and S.K. and that the information he gave was false.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant reiterated that he had sold books and silver accessories to a Greek official, L.K. and that this person had requested him to provide confidential information. He also contended that he had contacted L.K. and another Greek official, S.K., whom he knew as “Yorgo”, in order to maintain his business and that the information that he had given was false.

facts.text: The applicant’s representative argued that the applicant’s statements were taken under torture and referred to the medical report noting ecchymoses on his arms.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant’s representative stressed that the applicant’s statements had been taken under torture by MIT officers. She referred in this connection to the medical report dated 23 February 1998 prepared by the Davutpaşa military prison doctor who noted the presence of three to four day-old ecchymoses on the applicant’s arms.

facts.text: The applicant’s representative argued the telephone conversations were unlawfully obtained as there was no judicial authorization for tapping.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant’s representative also argued that the telephone conversations of the applicant, which were the sole evidence against him, had been obtained unlawfully by the MIT officers since there was no decision of a judge permitting them to tap his conversations on a public telephone.

facts.text: During proceedings, the General Staff Military Court summoned V.A.Ö. to give evidence but he could not be found.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  During the proceedings, the General Staff Military Court issued a summons requiring V.A.Ö. to give evidence. However, this person could not be found.

facts.text: A fingerprint expert analyzed the photographs and maps and found none of the fingerprints belonged to the applicant.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  On an unspecified date, a fingerprint expert conducted an analysis on the photographs and maps from the applicant’s shop. He observed that none of the fingerprints found belonged to the applicant.

facts.text: On 15 June 1999 the General Staff Military Court convicted the applicant of disloyalty to national defence by espionage and sentenced him to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  On 15 June 1999 the General Staff Military Court convicted the applicant as charged. The court considered that the information that the applicant had given could not be considered to be confidential. However, it held that, although the applicant had provided non-confidential or imaginary information in order to maintain his business contacts with the Greek officials, he had committed the offence of disloyalty to national defence by accepting their proposal to provide information. The court sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment, which was the minimum penalty prescribed by Article 56 § 1 (D) of the Military Criminal Code and Articles 133 § 1, 31, 33 and 36 of the Criminal Code.

facts.text: The court dismissed the applicant’s defence submissions but did not directly address his torture allegations or unlawful telephone tapping claims.

anchor.surface_text: While the court dismissed the applicant’s defence submissions, it did not address directly his allegations that his statements to the MIT officers had been obtained under torture and that his telephone conversations were unlawfully tapped by the MIT officers.

facts.text: On 2 August 1999 the applicant appealed, claiming innocence and arguing the conviction was based on unlawfully obtained evidence and lack of witness attendance.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  On 2 August 1999 the applicant appealed. He claimed that he was innocent of the crime since he had given false information to the Greek Intelligence Service and that he had never intended to betray his country. Relying on Article 6 of the Convention, the applicant further argued that the first instance court had convicted him on the basis of unlawfully obtained evidence, in particular the unlawful tapping and recording of his telephone conversations by the MIT. He also complained that the court had not secured the attendance of V.A.Ö as a witness. Referring to the medical report dated 23 February 1998 indicating ecchymoses on his arms, the applicant noted that the security forces had resorted to habitual methods to secure his conviction.

facts.text: On 17 November 1999 the Military Court of Cassation upheld the conviction, approving the first instance court’s reasoning and rejecting the appeal.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  On 17 November 1999 the Military Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 15 June 1999. It approved the reasoning of the first instance court’s judgment and noted that the latter had already accepted that the maps and photos had not belonged to the applicant and that it had not relied on the statements given by V.A.Ö. in the course of the preliminary investigation since he had not attended the trial. Accordingly, there was no deficiency or unlawfulness in the investigation leading to the applicant’s conviction. The court therefore rejected the applicant’s appeal.

facts.text: On 24 January 2000 the Military Court of Cassation’s decision was served on the applicant.

anchor.surface_text: 20.  On 24 January 2000 the Military Court of Cassation’s decision was served on the applicant.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that he had raised his complaint of ill-treatment before the domestic authorities in the course of the criminal proceedings against him but no action had been taken to investigate his allegations.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant submitted that he had raised his complaint of ill‑treatment before the domestic authorities in the course of the criminal proceedings against him but no action had been taken to investigate his allegations.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court considered that the applicant had done all that could be expected to bring his complaint to the authorities and dismissed the Government's objection to admissibility.

arguments.claim: The Government claimed that the applicant had failed to raise, even in substance, his complaints of ill-treatment before the national authorities and that therefore he had not availed himself of the remedies in domestic law.

anchor.surface_text: the Government claimed that the applicant had failed to raise, even in substance, his complaints of ill-treatment before the national authorities and that therefore he had not availed himself of the remedies in domestic law.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicant had raised the complaint sufficiently and the authorities failed to investigate, so the Government's objection was dismissed.

arguments.claim: The Government alleged that it had not been established with sufficient certainty that the ecchymoses observed on the applicant’s body had occurred during his detention in police custody and denied that the applicant had suffered ill-treatment during his detention in custody.

anchor.surface_text: The Government alleged that it had not been established with sufficient certainty that the ecchymoses observed on the applicant’s body had occurred during his detention in police custody since the prison doctor stated the ecchymoses were possibly three to four days old. They therefore denied that the applicant had suffered ill-treatment during his detention in custody.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt and found the applicant did not lay the basis of an arguable claim of ill-treatment due to lack of detail.

arguments.claim: The applicant alleged that the General Staff Court which tried him could not be regarded as an independent and impartial tribunal, given that it was composed of military judges bound by orders of the Ministry of Defence and general staff.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant alleged that the General Staff Court which tried him could not be regarded as an independent and impartial tribunal, given that it was composed of two military judges and an officer, all of whom were bound by the orders and instructions of the Ministry of Defence and the general staff which appointed them. In that connection he submitted that, as a civilian, he should not have been tried in a military court.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicant's doubts objectively justified given international consensus and the nature of the military court composition.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that only in exceptional circumstances was a civilian tried in a military court in Turkey and that the applicant was tried by a military court because he was charged with an offence concerning national security.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that only in exceptional circumstances was a civilian tried in a military court in Turkey. On that point, they maintained that the applicant was tried by a military court because he was charged with an offence concerning national security. The Government further maintained that the domestic law provided necessary safeguards to guarantee the independence and impartiality of military courts. Finally, they pointed out that, with the adoption of Law no. 4963, Turkish legislation had been amended to bring it into line with the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the legislation was insufficient to justify military court jurisdiction over civilians except in very exceptional circumstances, which were not substantiated here.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that the domestic courts had convicted him on the basis of his tape-recorded telephone conversations which had been unlawfully obtained by the MIT officers without judicial authorization.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant also complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the domestic courts had convicted him on the basis of his tape-recorded telephone conversations which had been unlawfully obtained by the MIT officers.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no domestic law regulated telephone tapping at the time, so the evidence was unlawfully obtained, but the overall proceedings were fair and rights of defence respected.

arguments.claim: The Government contended that the applicant’s telephone conversations had been tapped as part of MIT’s counter-intelligence activities permitted by law and that the measure complied with proportionality requirements.

anchor.surface_text: The Government contended that the applicant’s telephone conversations had been tapped in the framework of the MIT’s counter‑intelligence activities as permitted by Article 4 of Law no. 2937. Article 6 of the said law permitted MIT members to carry out counter‑intelligence activities and granted them the rights and powers enjoyed by the regular police. The MIT officers had decided to intercept and record the applicant’s conversations with a view to protecting national security. The measure in question had complied with the requirements of proportionality.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no legal basis existed domestically for telephone tapping at the time, so the Government's legal basis argument failed.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that the court had failed to hold a public hearing in violation of Article 6.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant complained that his right to a public hearing enshrined in Article 6 had also been violated.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court rejected the complaint for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies as the applicant did not raise it domestically.

arguments.claim: The Government noted that hearings before military courts were public but could be closed for public morality or security; exclusion was necessary for national security in this case.

anchor.surface_text: The Government noted that, according to Article 138 of the Military Court Organisation and Proceedings Law, hearings before military courts were public. However, the military court could hold hearings in camera if public morality and safety so required. In the instant case, since the applicant had been tried on charges of military espionage, exclusion of public was necessary for the purposes of national security.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that the trial court had failed to secure the attendance of V.A.Ö., an important witness for his defence.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant complained that he had been denied a fair hearing since the trial court had failed to secure the attendance of V.A.Ö. who could have testified for his defence.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the trial court summoned the witness but he could not be found and no failure to respect the right to a fair hearing occurred.

arguments.claim: The Government contended that the trial court had made sufficient efforts to secure the attendance of the witness but he could not be found.

anchor.surface_text: The Government contended that the trial court had made sufficient efforts to secure the attendance of the witness in question. However, he could not be found.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the Government's contention that sufficient efforts were made to secure the witness's attendance.
